reference.source: ISSVA classification / Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies
clinicalPearls: An abnormal venous communication connecting the intracranial dural venous sinuses to extracranial scalp veins through a defect in the skull
Presents as a soft, bluish, compressible scalp swelling, often near the midline over the frontal or parietal region
The lesion characteristically enlarges with manoeuvres that raise venous pressure (Valsalva, bending forward, crying) and empties on compression or when upright
It can be congenital or acquired following trauma, and may be isolated or associated with other venous or developmental anomalies
Cross-sectional imaging with venous phase (CT venography or MRI/MRV) demonstrates the transcalvarial venous connection
A key management concern is whether the lesion is dominant for intracranial venous drainage, which affects safety of intervention
Complications include cosmetic concern, bleeding with trauma, and rarely air embolism or infection
Management is individualised, ranging from observation to surgical or endovascular treatment after defining venous drainage
reference.pathophysiology: Sinus pericranii is a venous anomaly in which a direct, valveless communication forms between the intracranial dural venous sinuses and the extracranial veins of the scalp, passing through one or more defects (emissary channels) in the skull. Blood flows bidirectionally through this connection so that the extracranial venous pouch fills when intracranial venous pressure rises and empties with compression or upright posture. The anomaly may be developmental or arise after trauma, and its clinical significance hinges on whether it merely drains scalp veins or also carries important intracranial venous outflow.
additionalDifferentials: Dermoid or epidermoid cyst of the scalp
Eosinophilic granuloma or other lytic skull lesion
Aneurysmal bone cyst of the calvarium
additionalInvestigations: MRI with MR venography to characterise the venous anatomy
CT and CT venography to define the calvarial defect and transosseous channel
Catheter venography when detailed drainage assessment is needed before intervention
Doppler ultrasound to demonstrate compressibility and venous flow
Assessment of whether the sinus is dominant for intracranial drainage
Skull radiographs may show the bony defect
redFlags: Evidence that the lesion provides dominant intracranial venous drainage, raising risk with intervention
Significant bleeding after minor trauma to the swelling
Signs of air embolism or intracranial complication
Associated developmental venous anomalies affecting cerebral drainage
Rapid change in size or new neurological symptoms
reference.prognosis: Many lesions are stable and can be observed with a good prognosis; when treatment is indicated for cosmetic, symptomatic or safety reasons, outcomes are generally favourable provided the venous drainage pattern is defined beforehand to avoid compromising intracranial outflow.
pitfalls: Intervening without first establishing whether the sinus is dominant for intracranial venous drainage
Mistaking it for a simple cyst or cephalohaematoma and attempting incision
Overlooking the diagnostic positional and Valsalva-related size change
Failing to consider associated venous or developmental anomalies
references: Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies: Haemangiomas and Malformations
